summary: Gives suggestions and guidance for designing the tables and algorithms a host needs to keep track of names, addresses, ports and routes inside a TCP/IP implementation. It is advice, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer has to keep notes on who is who and where to send things. This memo advises how to organize those notes.

questions: tcp ip names addresses ports routes
why are ports not part of ip
how does a host find a gateway
how does ip decide where to send a datagram
subtitle: Clark's 1982 advice on the tables a TCP/IP host needs to keep track of names, addresses, ports and routes.

tldr.problem: A TCP/IP host refers to things by names, addresses, port identifiers and routes, and the old approach of keeping a complete static table for each does not scale to a much larger internet.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC advises caching instead of exhaustive tables: a name cache backed by name servers, a cache of address-to-gateway routes corrected by ICMP redirects, and a single dispatch algorithm on addresses, protocol number and ports.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational design memo with no protocol requirements, written to guide implementers in 1982, and it also explains why ports live in TCP and UDP rather than in IP.

today: RFC 814 is an Informational memo from July 1982 and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it. It is design advice rather than a specification, and it describes the internet as it stood then.

sections.title: Four Kinds of Identifiers
sections.content:
TCP/IP refers to things in several ways. People use character-string names for networks, hosts and services. Host names are translated into addresses, 32-bit values that identify the network and the host on it. Service names are translated into a port identifier, which is a 16-bit value in TCP. Addresses are in turn translated into routes, the sequence of steps a packet must take. The RFC gives suggestions for the tables and algorithms a host implementation needs to keep track of all of these.

It sizes the problem for its time. The internet then had no more than 25 active networks and a few hundred hosts, but implementers should assume an upper limit of about 1,000 networks. At an average of 25 hosts per net that is a maximum of 25,000 hosts, which is enough to make the current table management strategies unacceptable.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer has nicknames for places, house numbers, doors inside the house, and roads to get there. This memo is about keeping all of those lists tidy.

sections.title: Names and Name Servers
sections.content:
A static table translating every name to an address stops working with so many names: they change too fast for an installer to keep up, and most refer to machines the host will never talk to. The internet was moving from a single name table kept by the NIC and distributed to all hosts to a distributed approach, where each network or group of networks runs a name server. Each host stores only a cache of recently used names and asks a name server when a name is missing.

Because name servers were not yet in place, hosts still needed a complete table. The advice is to hide that table behind a subroutine interface so it can later be replaced by code that calls remote name servers. The RFC also warns that cached addresses can go stale when a host moves, and says plans were under way for a facility to query an address and learn what name is actually associated with it. SMTP already defines a verification technique along those lines.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of carrying a phone book for the whole world, keep a short list of numbers you called lately, and ask the operator when you need a new one.

sections.title: Addresses and Routes
sections.content:
When sending a datagram, IP compares the network number of the destination with its own. If they match, the packet goes directly to the recipient. Otherwise it goes to a gateway, and if several are available a second decision is needed. Early implementations used a table with 256 entries, one per possible network, because 8 bits identified the network, but the current address format has three network numbering options, so an exhaustive table is no longer possible.

The recommended strategy is a local cache of routing information. IP extracts the network number from the destination address and looks for a known gateway. If there is none, it picks any accessible gateway at random, records it, and sends the packet. If the guess is wrong, that gateway returns an ICMP redirect naming a better one, and the table is updated. The table size should follow the number of active connections the host supports: 100 or more entries for a large time sharing system, one for a personal computer with a single telnet connection. Failure of a gateway is covered in RFC 816.

How a new host first finds its gateways is deliberately left outside the internet architecture, since networks differ. Some allow a broadcast, some have special mechanisms, and sometimes an installer must supply one gateway name. After that the host can learn others from ICMP messages.
sections.plainLanguage: If the house is on your street, walk there. If not, hand the letter to any neighbor who goes to town. If that neighbor knows a better way, they tell you, and you remember it.

sections.title: Source Routes and Advanced Routing
sections.content:
A minimal implementation is enough for operational service, but research hosts need more, and all implementers are urged to leave a structure into which extra features can later be added. These include the IP source route options, a proposed form of ICMP redirect that applies to a particular host rather than a net, and proposed IP options to mark unacceptable routes.

Because these features apply to a particular connection, their use must be specified at the TCP level, so the interface between IP and the layers above must pass this information both ways. ICMP messages can arrive at any time, so an extra channel is needed between TCP and IP besides sending and receiving data. Users should be able to hand a source route to TCP when opening a connection. A listening TCP must be ready to receive a datagram carrying an IP return route, remember it, and use it as a source route on all returning datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes a traveler wants to choose the exact roads. The computer should be able to accept those directions, and remember the route a visitor took so it can reply the same way.

sections.title: Ports and Service Identifiers
sections.content:
IP only dispatches an arriving datagram to a protocol. The protocol handler, such as TCP, then dispatches it to the right connection using port identifiers in its own header. Putting IP in the kernel and TCP in a user program can cost heavy performance because of the extra dispatch, and the RFC says an acceptable shortcut is to move the higher level dispatching into the IP layer if that makes implementation easier (see RFC 817). For TCP and UDP the dispatch uses the foreign internet address, the protocol number, and the local and foreign ports. UDP dispatch is a subset: it depends only on protocol number and local port, the same subset TCP needs for a listen from any foreign host.

The RFC explains why ports are not part of IP. Protocols disagreed on port size, since TCP chose 16 bits to keep its header short while others wanted perhaps 32. Well known ports, such as TCP port 23 for remote login, would have needed central assignment for all of IP. And gateways would have been implied to need port knowledge, which they do not. A rendezvous server design was rejected because it would hurt isolated UDP datagrams. One constraint remains: an ICMP error returns only the IP header and the next 64 bits of the original datagram, so port information must sit in the first 64 bits of the higher level header.
sections.plainLanguage: The street address gets a letter to the right building. The port is the apartment number inside. The post office only needs the street address, so the apartment number is left to the building.
